 Debt in the heart of Texas: the struggle with student loans
 BY 
 Brian Scott
 Texas 
 PUBLISHED 10:00 AM CT Nov. 10, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 10:00 AM CST Nov. 10, 2026 
 SHARE 
 RICHARDSON, Texas — Saidah Fletcher once thought she would never shake years of student debt. But just two years ago, she threw a party to celebrate paying it off. Her friends and family helped her tear paper copies of her loan statements to shreds.
 “I brought them at the party and gave them out to everybody, and I said ‘rip em!’” Fletcher said with a laugh.
 Fletcher’s excitement is understandable when you learn just how deep she was into those debts. The Richardson woman was paying for not one, but two stints in higher education.
 “I had to borrow for my bachelor’s and my master's,” Fletcher said.
 Add in living expenses during school piled onto credit cards, and she was on the hook for a total of about $128,000. Fletcher said much of that came in the form of private loans that she signed while still a high school student, as most student loan recipients do.
 “I mean, my parents did raise us very to be very financially aware and smart. However, I just thought, okay, well, I'll just sign on the dotted line,” said Fletcher. “I don’t really think I understood the amount of how much, like how much it was really going to be.”
 But when she got out of college and entered the work world, it didn’t take long for the true amount of that debt to really set in for her. She was just starting her "adult life" and was already thousands of dollars behind — with the interest building daily.
 “It made me feel sick actually sometimes,” she said.
 Nearly 4 million Texans hold federal student loans totaling more than $138 billion, according to Department of Education data. The data also shows Texas leads the nation in number of borrowers and trails only California in total outstanding balance. Both states, however, have some of the largest populations in the country.
 The student debt problem stands, though, in every state. About 1 in 6 Americans holds a federal student loan, according to government data reviewed by Spectrum News. That doesn’t count private borrowers. The Education Data Initiative says Americans owe about $1.86 trillion in student debt.
 Martin Lynch, president of the Financial Counseling Association of America, said the situation is worsening.
 “There’s no income level that’s absent from that discussion, unfortunately,” Lynch said.
 He said recent Trump administration changes to federal loans, including to income-based repayment plans, add to the confusion.
 “It’s just getting worse. Student loan repayments are really causing a lot of difficulty for folks. Folks who are in default with those loans, total is just doubled to 10 million,” Lynch said. “It’s a difficult situation.”
 Lynch said his counselors work every day to help ease that burden, and the burden of debts in general, by renegotiating interest rates and building budgets. He said credit counseling is just one of many potential routes people can take to get help with their debt, but he urges those who are struggling to not take it on alone.
 “A service like ours, which is pretty painless, will help. It's not for everybody either, but people need to know that their toolbox has more than one tool,” he said.
 Experts say the worst thing people can do is try to ignore the debt and hope it will just go away, because it won’t.
 Fletcher certainly didn’t ignore her student debt; she said that was never an option for her as the weight of those debts was too much to sit with.
 “I really hustled maybe a little bit too much,” Fletcher said. “I said, no, I don’t want this to be my life.”
 She said she worked three jobs and pinched every penny for years, staying in while friends went out and missing out on experiences more than once.
 But it paid off, and two years ago she threw that "debt-free" party to celebrate her final payments.
 “I had a '90s party,” she said. “I got custom piñatas of those debtors, filled them with candy, and everyone had an opportunity to beat it.”
 Of course, Fletcher delivered the first blows herself.
 “I had someone hold it [the piñatas], and they’re like, ‘whoa you’re kinda strong,’ and I’m like, ‘it’s been 10 years in the making!’” Fletcher said.
 While the path was lonely at times, Fletcher said she doesn’t regret the way she buckled down, especially as she sees many friends continue to struggle with their own student debts. Now, after years of struggling and paying, she’s debt free and not going back.
 “And I felt alone a lot of the times because people my age and my early 30s are like, ‘Why, why are you doing this? Don’t worry,’ I’m like, no, this is I can’t I can’t let this linger,” she said.
